tools.name: get_scene
tools.description:
Get the current scene tree. Each object includes `enabled` (self state), `visible` (effective 鈥?false if any ancestor is hidden), and `renderOrder` (0-based hierarchy order; larger means rendered later/on top). By default returns summary (names, GUIDs, component types, mesh bounds, camera info) 鈥?use summary=false for full property values.

Scale controls for large scenes (compose together): `subtree` (a GUID) returns only that object and its descendants; `depth` (>=1) keeps only that many object levels (render-group children are level 1) and marks elided branches with `_childrenTruncated`; `names_only:true` returns a {guid,name,children} skeleton 鈥?the cheapest way to see the hierarchy shape, then drill in with `inspect` or a `subtree` call.

Returns STATIC EDITOR data 鈥?does NOT reflect runtime script changes. To observe runtime state, use interact_by_dsl with screenshot or get_script_logs.

Call after create/open project and after completing the static scene (before adding scripts).

summary.description: If true (default), return compact summary without component property values. Set to false for full details.

subtree.description: A scene object GUID. Return only that object and its descendants (scoped before depth/names_only). Errors if the GUID is not in the scene.

depth.description: Keep only this many object levels (>=1; render-group children are level 1). Objects at the limit drop their children and gain `_childrenTruncated` (count elided). Use to skim a deep hierarchy.

names_only.description: Return a minimal {guid, name, children} skeleton per object (no components/bounds). Cheapest hierarchy overview; combine with subtree/depth.

tools.name: get_scene_view
tools.description: Capture the editor Scene panel as a PNG plus a JSON annotation sidecar mapping each scene object to its screen-pixel bounds. All 2D colliders are temporarily forced visible during the capture so their wireframes appear in the image 鈥?use this to self-verify collider alignment against the visual mesh, then iterate. Returns content as [image PNG, JSON text]. The JSON sidecar shape is {view: {mode, width, height}, objects: [{guid, name, screenBounds:{x,y,w,h}, screenBoundsNorm:{x,y,w,h}, colliderType?, colliderPoints?}], notes?}. COORDINATES: screenBounds are PIXELS of the attached Scene-panel image (top-left origin) and screenBoundsNorm is the same rect normalized to [0,1] OF THAT IMAGE 鈥?neither is a preview tap coordinate (the Scene camera pans/zooms independently of the preview frame). To tap a 2D object, derive the point from its ScreenTransform (anchoredPosition/sizeDelta at 720x1280, center origin y-up: tapX = 0.5 + X/720, tapY = 0.5 - Y/1280). Entries whose screenBounds are ~1px are origin markers for objects with no renderer/collider bounds, not real rects. For runtime debugging (script-driven state) use interact_by_dsl with screenshot instead 鈥?this tool reads the static editor scene.

maxSize.description: Maximum pixel length of the longer image side (default 1024). The image is downsized via sharp if the panel exceeds this; screenBounds are scaled accordingly.

objectGuids.description: Optional subset of scene-object GUIDs to annotate. Omit to annotate every object in the scene.

tools.description:

Scripts include `class_name` and `is_component` (whether the engine registered it as a usable component 鈥?false means the decorator is wrong). SourceFiles (FBX, MP4/GIF) are grouped under "SourceFile".

Automatically includes `_annotation` for previously annotated assets. For texture assets WITHOUT annotations, preview images are returned inline so you can see what they are.

IMPORTANT: After receiving preview images, you MUST call annotate() with descriptions for ALL un-annotated textures.

type_filter.description: Filter by resource type (e.g., "Material", "Texture", "Mesh", "Script", "SourceFile"). Omit to list all; an unmatched filter reports which types the project does have.

preview_offset.description: Offset into the list of un-annotated textures needing preview (default 0). Auto-previews are paged to keep the response small; after annotating the current batch, call again with the returned `_previewNextOffset` to fetch the next page. Annotated textures drop out of the set, so the loop converges.

tools.name: inspect
tools.description:
Inspect any GUID 鈥?automatically identifies whether it is a SceneObject, Component, Resource, or SourceFile and returns full information.

For SceneObjects: returns renderOrder, components with all property values, mesh bounds, camera info. Children are listed shallow ({guid, name}) 鈥?call inspect on a child GUID to drill in.

For Resources: returns type, provider, and properties.
For Prefab assets: additionally attaches `rootSceneObject` 鈥?the prefab's stored hierarchy (enriched + unified naming, without scene renderOrder). Pass `summary: true` to collapse it to a compact tree when the prefab is deep.

tools.name: read_visual_scripting_graph
tools.description:
Read the project's visual scripting graphs. Covers ALL THREE containers: the project graph (the node graph authored in the Visual Scripting panel, Graph/graph.json), every Custom Component Graph asset (reusable graphs attached to objects, Assets/**/*.compgraph), AND every Subgraph asset (reusable node groups, Assets/**/*.ssubgraph). Returns a compact tree of containers 鈫?nodes (with their ports, configured port values, and edges), recursing into Group subgraphs. Component types and property names are returned as unified names.

Use this to understand or port visual scripting to APJS 鈥?it replaces hand-parsing Graph/graph.json and unzipping .compgraph / .ssubgraph assets.

The project graph appears under top-level `containers`; Custom Component Graphs under `componentGraphs[]` (each with `name`, `path`, `containers`); Subgraph assets under `subgraphs[]` (each with `name`, `path`, `interface` = the reuse `inputPorts`/`outputPorts`, and `graph` = the inner nodes/edges). A Subgraph's per-instance tuning values live on the collapsed Group port values at each USE SITE in the project graph, not in the asset definition.

Visual scripting is LEGACY and READ-ONLY: use this to understand a graph, never to author or modify one. To move a graph project forward, add co-existing APJS or port the graph to APJS (see skills/VisualScriptingGraph).

Returns STATIC on-disk data; if the user just edited a graph in the panel without saving, the file may be slightly stale. Returns {hasGraph: false} when the project has no project graph and no graph assets.

Port/node Guid(...) references (targetGuid, or Entity/Component port values) map directly to the matching guid in Assets/main.scene.

container_id.description: Only return the container with this id (from a prior read_visual_scripting_graph call). Omit to return all containers.

full.description: Return the raw parsed graph JSON instead of the compact summary (large 鈥?use only when the summary omits a field you need).

tools.name: query_knowledge
tools.description:
Search the TTEH knowledge base before unfamiliar scene, component, resource, asset, template, or scripting work. Use one focused call per category; for multiple independent lookups, call this tool in parallel.

Use `query` for broad discovery in English. Use exact lookup params when you already know the target name.

Categories:
- "component": component schemas and DSL wire-format help. Use `component_type` for exact lookup, or `query` to search.
- "object": built-in scene object types. Use returned `object_type` with `add_builtin_object`.
- "skill": topic guides and script examples. Use `query` to search skill catalog metadata; use `skill_categories` for exact SkillId lookup; use `tags` for script examples.
- "resource": asset operations, resource creation, resource schemas, and built-in resources. Use `resource_type` for exact lookup, or `query` to search.
- "game_asset": local importable asset files. Use `query` or `tags`.

For game-design / mechanic / template / visual-inspiration lookups, use the dedicated `search_game_design` tool instead.

query.description: English search phrase for broad discovery.

component_type.description: Specific component type name (for category="component"). E.g., "Camera", "Transform".

resource_type.description: Specific resource type name (for category="resource"). E.g., "StandardPBR".

tools.name: search_game_design
tools.description:
Semantic search over the game mechanic catalog. Each mechanic represents a gameplay rule loop and carries **buildables** (DSL scaffolds you can apply via `apply_template`) and **visualReferences** (curated themes / concept art for borrowing layout + palette). Returns a single ranked list with per-mechanic tier (strong / weak).

Replaces the previous two-call pattern of `query_knowledge(category="game_template")` + `query_visual_inspiration` 鈥?one call covers both surfaces.

Uses all-MiniLM-L6-v2 sentence embeddings over each mechanic's `name + family + tags + gameplay`. Mechanics inspired by well-known external games carry the analogue in their text (e.g. "Whack-a-mole style", "Angry Birds style") so queries using those names bridge naturally.

**Decision per mechanic**:
- Strong tier AND your design's gameplay loop / win-lose / primary input all match the buildable 鈫?`apply_template`, then adapt theme / assets / params on top.
- Strong tier BUT the core mechanic diverges (you'd have to rip out the scaffold's defining behaviour) 鈫?do NOT apply. Build your own and borrow specific elements / visuals. Applying a half-fit scaffold leaves the wrong core mechanic to patch around.
- Weak tier 鈫?do not apply; borrow individual visual elements / layout only.
- Borrowing (either tier) 鈫?record it via `mechanic_refs: [{mechanic_id, borrowed_elements: [...]}]`. `mechanic_id` is the MECHANIC id (result heading), never a buildable id 鈥?buildable ids belong only in `starter_template.template_id`.

**MANDATORY for new/full game builds or major rebuilds** 鈥?call once with the gameplay loop + theme as the query, before `save_plan(type="game")`.

Phrase `query` as natural-language gameplay intent ("paddle bouncing balls into brick wall", "tap to drop merging fruit", "spin a wheel of my friends"). Token-stuffing is unnecessary.

query.description: Natural-language gameplay intent + theme. Examples: "tap to merge falling fruit", "AR head-tilt quiz", "slingshot at friend tower", "endless lane-switch runner".

max_results.description: Maximum mechanics returned across both tiers (default 12). Use a small number (5鈥?) for top picks; raise to 20+ for the full weak-tier tail.

tools.name: save_plan
tools.description:
Save or update the project handoff plan.

Before persisting type="game": confirm the design reflects what the user asked for, not intent you guessed from a thin prompt. This tool validates that the plan is complete and consistent, NOT that it is the effect the user wanted 鈥?a well-formed plan for the wrong game still passes. If the core loop, win/lose, primary input, or interaction targets rest on a guess, clarify with one closed-ended question first (see AGENTS.md Rule #0 / Screening); do not encode a guess as the contract.

Read skills/Planning/SKILL.md before calling this tool. Both plan types require scene_representation so the 2D/3D construction decision, layers, requirements, limitations, and verification evidence are explicit before scene editing. Submit the complete Phase 2 plan in one call; do not use this for local changes that preserve the existing contract.

Preferred scene item shapes: requirements[] = {id, description, must}; layers[] = {id, role, description, space, content_form, requirement_refs}; verification[] = {id, description, requirement_refs, views_or_states, success_criteria}. Layer and verification requirement_refs are the input source of truth; reciprocal references are derived before canonical validation and persistence. Compact descriptor strings and success_criteria string arrays are normalized automatically.

High-risk pre-submit checklist (complete rule list lives in skills/Planning/SKILL.md and the input schema): include starter_template using one of two modes 鈥?{mode: "selected", template_id} when a strong-tier buildable has a core loop + win/lose + primary input that all match your design and you apply it (then adapt theme/assets on top), or {mode: "none", rationale} when no scaffold core loop matches and you build from scratch; borrow specific elements/visuals from search results via mechanic_refs regardless of mode; include mechanic_refs (from search_game_design) OR mechanic_rationale (>=30 chars); each borrowed_elements entry must be reflected in assets/screens/interactions; include record_start_reset and retry interactions; include a result screen with a retry element; if any asset has is_background: true, set camera_feed_constraints.composition: segmentation_portrait and composition_option; if game_type.camera_feed: hidden, include camera_feed_hidden_rationale (>=30 chars, based on prompt rejection + reason); keep assets[].id and screens[].layout[].id unique when present, and make interaction target ids reference those ids; gameplay_action should include feedback.visual.

Do not continue to Phase 3, asset sourcing, scene build, scripting, review, or apply_template until type="game" returns success: true. Warnings persist but indicate risks to fix when practical.

Use type="general" with scene_representation and content for non-game plans. Unknown requirement, space, and content-form values are accepted; prefer custom.* names and place experimental metadata under extensions. Missing fallback behavior defaults to adapt_and_verify for unknown requirements and stop_and_explain for unmet must requirements. Use log(level="summary") for final built-state handoff summaries.

tools.name: get_script_logs
tools.description: Read the orionkit console log buffer 鈥?covers APJS script runtime output, script compile diagnostics, AUSL shader compile errors (`[AUSLCompiler]`), and material import logs (`[MaterialImporter]`). Despite the name, this tool is the generic console-log reader for any compile/runtime signal the engine emits. For routine checks after add_script/import_glsl, prefer the auto-collected `_compileCheck` field on the edit_by_dsl response. After a native `.omtl` edit, run get_material_status through edit_by_dsl instead. Call this tool when you need raw console context (e.g., what logs surrounded the error) or when _compileCheck is missing. source.description: Log source filter: "compile" for compile/import diagnostics (TypeScript errors, AUSL shader errors, MaterialImporter messages) 鈥?"runtime" for console.log and runtime output only 鈥?"all" for everything (default: "all")

limit.description: Maximum number of log entries to return (default: 50)

since.description: High-water fence: return only entries newer than this ISO-8601 timestamp (or epoch ms). The console buffer is machine-global and cumulative (a reload never clears it), so without a fence a read mixes this run with stale/foreign lines from other projects and sessions. Snapshot a fence before a reload/interaction (e.g. the newest entry's `time`) and pass it here after to get only this run's logs. Runtime entries carry second-precision times, so the fence keeps everything from the fence's own second onward 鈥?the snapshot entry itself may reappear; treat re-seen lines as already handled. tools.name: capture_preview
tools.description: Verify the live preview in one call: reloads the scene (reset_preview), waits for the requested post-reload preview texture updates, then captures a screenshot and returns the image inline. This is the default way to visually verify a build after scene edits, scripts, assets, or layout changes 鈥?use it instead of hand-assembling reset_preview + screenshot via interact_by_dsl. The default 5-frame barrier reduces stale or transitional captures but does not guarantee that asynchronous algorithms, tracking, models, large resources, or delayed script behavior are ready. Increase post_reload_frames up to 30 for those effects, and use later wait + screenshot checkpoints when the result is absent, changing, or suspicious. For interactive verification that needs taps/drags/timing, use interact_by_dsl.

post_reload_frames.description: Number of preview texture updates to observe after the matching reload acknowledgement before taking the screenshot. Defaults to 5; increase it for effects that depend on asynchronous algorithms, tracking, models, or large resources.

tools.name: apply_template

tools.name: generate_image
tools.description: Generate a new 2D image asset and import it into the asset panel. Parallel-safe: when you need N independent images, launch N generate_image calls concurrently in the same turn rather than one at a time. Preferred source for visuals 鈥?main characters, key props, theme-specific backgrounds, anything the user named or themed ("feed the cat", "space background"). `generate_image` produces higher-quality, unique, theme-matched art versus generic library stock. For **commodity visuals** (standard HUD icons, generic stickers, stock particles) prefer `search_library` instead 鈥?it is zero-latency and library quality is already sufficient for non-distinctive assets. Supports three asset types: "sticker" (foreground with transparent background), "background" (full-frame image), "frame" (decorative border). IP / moderation: image generation has no built-in IP awareness and is *attracted* to famous, often-copyrighted designs 鈥?naming or even obliquely evoking a known character (e.g. "Mario-inspired", or "a cartoon plumber with a red hat and an M") tends to reproduce it and will cause an image generation failure from content moderation. Moderation judges the OUTPUT image, not just the prompt 鈥?concepts strongly tied to a franchise (masks, uniforms, iconic silhouettes) can be rejected even with original wording. Prompt for an *original* design that fits the spirit of the request; on a moderation rejection, rework toward a clearly different design and retry 鈥?do not resubmit the same prompt. Returns a 360px preview image plus {asset:{guid,name}, annotation:{source,description}}. After visually inspecting the returned image, call edit_by_dsl/annotate with what the image actually shows.

name.description: Short, descriptive name for the generated asset (e.g. "RedCar", "NeonBolt", "FloralFrame"). Used as the asset file name in the editor.

tools.name: generate_gif
tools.description: Generate an animated sticker (GIF) asset and import it into the asset panel as a Texture Sequence. Two-phase & asynchronous: this call submits the job and returns a task_id 鈥?it does NOT block until the animation is ready. The animation is driven by a single first frame: either pass an existing image asset via `input_asset_guid` (e.g. one you just made with generate_image), or omit it and provide a `prompt` (+ optional style/aspect_ratio) to auto-generate the first frame. The auto first frame is rendered on a plain gray background and is NOT pre-cut 鈥?final transparency is applied once to the animation per `cutout`, which yields cleaner results than animating an imperfect cutout. `motion_prompt` describes how the subject should move/animate. `duration` is the clip length in seconds (2-5, default 3). `cutout` (default true) keeps a transparent background (subject cutout); set false to keep the generated background. Output aspect ratio always follows the first frame (keep_ratio) 鈥?there is no ratio control. IP / moderation rules are identical to generate_image: prompt for an ORIGINAL design; a moderation rejection on the first frame or the animation means rework, not resubmit. Returns {task_id, first_frame:{guid,generated}} 鈥?then poll query_gif_task({task_id, name, motion_prompt}) roughly every 30s until it reports success or failure. Do other useful work between polls; never busy-wait.

name.description: Short, descriptive name for the generated animated asset (e.g. "WavingCat", "SpinningCoin"). Used as the asset file name.

motion_prompt.description: Describes how the subject should move/animate (e.g. "the cat waves its paw and blinks"). Required.

input_asset_guid.description: Optional. GUID of an existing image asset to use as the animation first frame. For the best GIF quality, use an image with a clean, solid gray background, a fully-visible subject, and crisp edges with NO white outline / die-cut border (NOT a pre-cut transparent sticker, NOT a busy scene) 鈥?final transparency is applied later per `cutout`. If omitted, a first frame is auto-generated from `prompt` on a plain gray background.

prompt.description: Text prompt for the first-frame image, used only when `input_asset_guid` is omitted. Describe the subject/appearance in POSITIVE terms only (its motion goes in `motion_prompt`). Do NOT add negative phrases like "no border", "no white outline", or "no background" 鈥?image models do not honor negation and will render exactly the things you name.

style.description: First-frame visual style (only when generating the first frame). Defaults to "General".

aspect_ratio.description: First-frame aspect ratio (only when generating the first frame). Defaults to "1:1".

duration.description: Clip length in seconds (2-5). Defaults to 3.

cutout.description: Keep a transparent background (subject cutout). Defaults to true.
